Montreal police will be providing an update Tuesday on the scandal surrounding Station 39 in the city's Montréal-Nord borough following allegations of racial profiling by a group of officers.

The Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) made the allegations public in June, during an unprecedented late-night news conference headed by Chief Fady Dagher.

Dagher revealed that 16 officers at Station 39 were being investigated for racist and hateful acts allegedly committed against Black and Arab people during police stops.

As a result, Dagher announced the 16-member patrol was being disbanded.

The probe was launched after colleagues of the officers reported the behaviour, he said.

SPVM to discuss plans to fight racism

Tuesday’s public meeting was initially scheduled for July 8, but was pushed back after an active shooter situation in Montreal led to the deaths of three people, including a police officer.

The meeting will start at 6 p.m. at city hall and is open to members of the public. It will be streamed online.

The SPVM’s presentation to the city’s public security commission will provide more details on the alleged misconduct of several Station 39 officers.

It will also touch on the SPVM's intent to change its culture, and its response plan for the Montréal-Nord police station.



Members of the public will then be allowed to ask questions provided they have registered before the end of the presentation.

Those attending remotely can register online here . In-person attendees can register online ahead of time, or onsite at the welcome desk in front of the Salle des Armoiries starting at 5:30 p.m.

Community groups hope for accountability

When the scandal broke, community leaders and Montréal-Nord residents expressed their outrage, but said they were not surprised by the allegations, noting that racial profiling is not a new problem.

WATCH | Study shows racial profiling by Montreal police: Black, Arab people stopped by Montreal police at disproportionately high rates, new data shows | Duration 2:57 Amid allegations of racist and hateful acts by 16 police officers in Montréal-Nord, a new study shows that, in the city, Black people are four times more likely to be stopped than white individuals, while Arab people are five times more likely to be stopped.

Dardia Joseph, a lawyer and deputy director with the Clinique Juridique de Saint-Michel — a non-profit legal aid clinic — said she’s hoping Tuesday’s meeting will reflect that.

“This is not the first time that we have this conversation,” she said, referring to a public hearing in front of the commission in 2024. “My hope for this meeting is that we don’t start as if we are beginning from zero.”

She said that although the SPVM updated its street check policy in 2025 to include monitoring and evaluation measures, she hopes officials will clarify what has actually changed since those new guidelines were introduced.

Joseph questioned why the SPVM remains committed to street checks, given that nothing has changed and the practice is known to lead to discriminatory outcomes.

Joseph, along with other community leaders, demanded concrete action. She noted that she has yet to hear an apology to the residents of Montréal-Nord or "the youths who are being targeted," adding that the community wants to see real accountability.

Rebuilding public trust

Other agenda items for Tuesday’s public meeting focus on rebuilding community trust through direct outreach and engagement.

Fo Niemi is the director of the Center for Research-Action on Race Relations (CRARR) — a human rights advocacy group.

He said when it comes to incidents like those in Montréal-Nord, it’s important to have complete transparency and include the perspective of those who are affected.

“We have to be very citizen oriented. We have to be also very victim centred in looking at the situation in Montreal North and see how they have been or to what extent they have been affected by police bias,” he said.

Another local group, the Regroupement des intervenants et intervenantes d’origine haïtienne, issued several recommendations ahead of Tuesday’s meeting aimed at regaining that trust.

Among them is having Station 39 be under civilian command, and the creation of an independent citizen oversight committee with a clear mandate for monitoring, documentation and accountability.

The group also recommends aligning public safety goals with social and economic development, because the issues are often intertwined.

Lastly they recommend that those found responsible for serious racist or hateful acts face sanctions that are proportionate to the gravity of the actions.

To date, three of the 16 police officers at Station 39 have been suspended, three were reassigned to administrative duties and the others were transferred to different units within the police department, as reported by the Canadian Press.

Dagher also said in June that possible criminal charges could be brought against some officers.

Quebec's Director of Criminal and Penal Prosecutions (DPCP) told CBC News in a statement that Montreal police hadn't, to date, submitted any requests to initiate criminal proceedings against any officers.

"Consequently, there is currently no file under review by the DPCP for analysis and charge authorization regarding the events addressed in the SPVM’s press conference on June 12, 2026," the statement reads.

The DPCP, however, noted that allegations had been submitted for review, as required by the Police Act, and that SPVM investigators are in contact with prosecutors to seek legal advice regarding their investigation.

World.title: A murderer's truck sits in Sask. RCMP cold storage. The Crown says it's time to destroy it
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It's been 20 years since Curtis Dagenais murdered two Saskatchewan RCMP officers and injured a third, but later this month he will be back in court in Saskatoon.

Why? It's about his truck.

The 1986 blue GMC 1500 is still sitting in cold storage at RCMP headquarters in Regina. The Crown is applying to have it forfeited so it can be destroyed, but Dagenais is opposed.

Dagenais was in the truck on July 6, 2006, when three RCMP constables tried to arrest him in Spiritwood, about 147 kilometres north of Saskatoon. He drove off and led the officers, who were in two separate vehicles, on a chase over rural roads.

RCMP constables Marc Bourdages and Robin Cameron were in one vehicle, which rammed into the side of Dagenais's truck and pushed it up against a tree. Dagenais shot them both in the head and they died of their injuries in hospital.

Const. Michelle Knopp arrived on the scene just moments after her colleagues were shot. Dagenais shot and injured her.

Const. Robin Cameron, left, and Const. Marc Bourdages died in hospital after being shot while on duty on July 7, 2006. (RCMP)

A jury convicted Dagenais in 2009 of two counts of first-degree murder and one count of attempted murder. He received three sentences of life in prison with no chance of parole for 25 years (the parole eligibility date is calculated from the date of his arrest on July 17, 2006).

He appealed the convictions to the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal, which dismissed his appeal in a ruling issued in 2012.

Why is the truck issue in court now?

The question of why the forfeiture application wasn't made before was posed in court to Scott Bartlett, the Crown prosecutor who brought the application.

"I really can't answer that, other than it slipped through the cracks," Bartlett said.

Bartlett is one of the two prosecutors who ran the original trial in 2009. He first made the application for forfeiture in 2021, when it was heard by the trial judge, Justice Gerald Allbright, who is now retired.

(Bartlett said he is no longer employed full-time by public prosecutions, but still works under fee-for-service contracts as an agent for the Attorney General.)

Crown prosecutors Al Johnson, centre left, and Scott Bartlett speak to media following the verdict in Curtis Dagenais's trial in 2009 in Saskatoon. (Geoff Howe/The Canadian Press)

At the hearing in 2021, Dagenais said he didn't want the truck destroyed because he maintains he's innocent and the bullet holes in the truck can help prove it.

He said he had asked Innocence Canada — a non-profit organization that advocates for the exoneration of people who are wrongfully convicted — to help him.

Dagenais was on Innocence Canada's waiting list, and Allbright agreed to give Dagenais more time to see whether the organization would take on his case.

Allbright adjourned the Crown's forfeiture application and said it could be renewed any time after Nov. 30, 2022.

"If at that time, no progress has been made in the advancement of Mr. Dagenais's application to Innocence Canada, I am of the view that it would be appropriate for the court to make the forfeiture order which the Crown seeks," Allbright wrote in a fiat.

A court exhibit photo from Curtis Dagenais's trial in 2009 shows the front of an RCMP vehicle after it smashed into the side of Dagenais's blue truck. (Geoff Howe/The Canadian Press)

Crown renews application

The Crown brought the application forward again in May of this year, and a hearing was held in Saskatoon Court of King's Bench on June 25 — this time, in front of Justice Daryl Labach.

Dagenais, 61, attended by video conference from Saskatchewan Penitentiary, wearing a blue T-shirt and glasses. His short-cropped hair is greying at the temples.

Bartlett again represented the Crown, while Dagenais did not have a lawyer and represented himself.

Like he did in 2021, Dagenais said he was opposed to the forfeiture and destruction of the truck.

"I would like to keep it preserved," he said.

"There's a couple holes in that truck that can't be properly re-examined by photograph."

A view from inside the RCMP vehicle that struck Curtis Dagenais's truck on July 7, 2006, and the holes in the windshield from bullets fired that day. (Geoff Howe/Canadian Press)

Labach noted that Innocence Canada had filed a letter with the court indicating they were not representing Dagenais and would not be pursuing any kind of application on his behalf.

Dagenais asked for another adjournment to see if he can get a lawyer to help him oppose the forfeiture application.

"How long are you suggesting it should be adjourned for?" Labach asked.

"I don't know. The wheels seem to roll really slow around here," Dagenais said.

Labach noted that Dagenais's "only opportunity" to reopen his case would be an appeal to the minister of justice. He asked Bartlett for his thoughts.

Bartlett said Saskatchewan Justice has received "numerous requests, submissions" alleging Dagenais was wrongfully convicted and suggesting there was new evidence.

"Nothing of that has ever materialized or come to pass, in our opinion, and of course nothing has changed today," Bartlett said.

Labach said he was prepared to grant Dagenais one more adjournment to give him the chance to get a lawyer.

The forfeiture hearing is scheduled for Aug. 31.

World.title: Europe is getting hit with its 5th heat wave since May — and sunken Nazi warships are resurfacing
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Nazi German warships scuttled in the Danube River during the Second World War are resurfacing as water levels plunge — a striking sign of the extreme heat and drought gripping Europe this summer.

The fifth heat wave since May is set to scorch western Europe beginning Tuesday, with parts of Spain, France and Italy nearing 40 C before the heat dome pushes temperatures further above average in central and northern Europe.

The European Union's Copernicus climate monitoring service confirmed Monday that June and July were the hottest on record in western Europe. The period saw an estimated 25,000 heat-related deaths.

The sweltering heat has contributed to devastating wildfires and pushed water levels in vital waterways, including the Danube, to record lows.

Climate scientists say the exposed wrecks are a vivid sign of a much broader problem: fossil fuel-driven climate change is intensifying heat and drought, with consequences for wildfires, agriculture, shipping and energy systems across Europe.

"If we keep emitting greenhouse gases at the rate we're doing now, then this is only going to get worse," Richard Allan, a climate scientist at England's University of Reading, told CBC News.

And what we're seeing this summer, he says, is just the "tip of the iceberg" for the effects of global heating.

WATCH | Fossil fuel emissions made Canada's wildfires more likely, study says: Wildfires are more intense, more likely — and humans are to blame: study | Duration 2:05 Climate change caused by fossil fuel use made July's wildfires in parts of Canada twice as likely to occur, researchers say. The new World Weather Attribution study also predicts more frequent — and more intense — wildfires will be the new normal.

What the drying Danube reveals

Historians estimate that the Nazis scuttled up to 200 warships near the Serbian city of Prahovo in September 1944 in an effort to stop advancing Soviet forces.

The New York Times reports that one or two or the wrecks might normally be visible in summer, but residents have counted about a dozen this year.

Elsewhere, the drying Danube has revealed a German military motorcycle in Hungary, an unexploded 700-kilogram British bomb in Slovakia and what are believed to be the ancient remains of a mammoth in Bulgaria.

People view the wreckage of a German warship from the Second World War that emerged from beneath the Danube River, near Prahovo, not far from the Djerdap II dam between the border of Romania and Serbia. (Darko Vojinovic/The Associated Press)

But the extremely low water levels have raised much more urgent concerns for several countries along Europe's second-longest river.

The Danube originates in Germany and runs 2,850 kilometres through nine other countries — Austria, Slovakia, Hungary, Croatia, Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria, Moldova and Ukraine — before emptying into the Black Sea. Its tributaries extend into several other countries.

The Romanian government restricted water use for crop irrigation last month and has taken steps to keep its only working nuclear power plant running, including blowing up a rock obstruction to redirect the river's flow.

Hungary switched a turbine back on at its only nuclear power station Monday after citizens and companies voluntarily curbed their power use last week because the river's flow was too low to cool reactors.

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said Friday the "succession of unprecedented events," from the extreme heat to the severe water shortage and state of the Danube, has more people realizing "that we must take much better care of our natural resources, our water, our land and our clean air than we have done so far."

PHOTOS | Here's what the Danube River looks like as water levels drop amid record hot summer:

'Clear example' of climate change

In June and July 1944, in the months before German forces sank their warships in the Danube, temperatures in Europe were around average — and perhaps slightly cooler than normal — compared to the 1991-2020 average, according to NASA's National Centers for Environmental Information.

During the same period this year, the average surface air temperature across the western half of the continent was 2.79 C higher, Copernicus reported this week. Much of eastern Europe, including areas of the Danube River basin, was also much warmer than average.

"This is a clear example of how climate change is intensifying heat extremes, with heat and drought increasingly reinforcing one another," Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at Copernicus, said in its press release.

By the time a major river system such as the Danube reaches levels this low, Allan said, damage to forests and agriculture has already occurred.

"These big river systems are the last to go," he said. "That's like the end point in the sense that soils have already dried out, vegetation has already dried out and we've seen these massive wildfires."

Allan said next year could be even worse.

He said the emergence of what's been dubbed a super El Niño — a particularly stronger cyclical warming in the southern Pacific Ocean that affects global weather patterns — has not been a factor in the heat that has punished Europe and much of the Northern Hemisphere so far this summer.

Two of the German warship wrecks that have emerged in the stretch of the Danube river in Serbia. Residents of the nearby village of Prahovo say you might normally see one or two of the sunken vessels in summer but there are as many as 12 visible this year. (Darko Vojinovic/The Associated Press)

"Usually ... the planet will be warmer the year following the emergence of El Niño," he said. "So, we can expect very high, unprecedented global temperatures in 2027."

Those effects, Allan said, would come on top of the warming already being driven by climate-harming greenhouse gas emissions.

"If we keep emitting greenhouse gases at the rate we're doing now," he said, "this is only, like, the first signs of what's going to happen in the future."

World.title: Get ready for 'meteor Christmas' with an added bonus: a partial solar eclipse
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Every August we are treated to one of the best meteor showers of the year: the Perseids. This year, on the day of the shower's peak, we will also get a partial solar eclipse.

Let's start with the Perseids.

This shower is often considered one of the best, if not the best, of the year because of the number and brightness of its meteors, along with the usually favourable viewing weather.

The peak viewing night is Aug. 12-13, which is great news for meteor chasers: It coincides with a new moon, meaning there will be no pesky moonlight to interfere with faint meteors.

"The really cool thing this year is, I expect the Perseid grazers to be in full force," said Peter Brown, Canada Research Chair in Meteor Astronomy and a professor at Western University in London, Ont.

These are Earth-grazers — meteors that enter Earth's atmosphere and then head back into space. They can be bright and fast, making them quite spectacular to see.

(Note: The author saw an extremely bright Earth-grazer on the night of Aug. 3 from downtown Toronto.)

"I think people should plan on getting out early. You can start seeing Perseids around 10 [p.m.] — 9.30," Brown said. "I would try to get out as soon as you can in that window because I bet this year people are going to get to see at least a handful of these bright grazers."

This composite image shows several Perseid meteors streaking against the night sky with some fireflies, right, in 2021 from eastern Ontario. (Malcolm Park)

The shower is expected to peak around midnight Eastern Daylight Time, increasing the number of meteors visible each hour. Brown said there could be upwards of 120 an hour.

But don't expect to see that many. That estimate assumes ideal conditions at a dark-sky location.

Still, a higher overall rate increases the number people are likely to see.

"You're not going to see 120, but you'll probably see a dozen or 20 in the early evening, and many of those will probably be bright," Brown said.

‘Meteor Christmas'

You don't have to wait until the peak night to see Perseids. The shower began July 17, and the number of visible meteors increases each night as the peak of Aug. 12-13 approaches.

Check the forecast. If the peak night is expected to be cloudy, consider observing in the days beforehand.

"I focus on the night of the 12th, morning of the 13th — I mean, that is the best. But, you know, the 11th will probably be 80 per cent of the show," Brown said. "If it looks like the weather is better on the Tuesday night, it is totally worth going out."

He also noted that, statistically, the meteors tend to be brighter the night before the peak.

The first requirement for seeing as many meteors as possible is a clear sky. If conditions co-operate, find the darkest location you can.

Stay off your phone: Its light will interfere with your eyes' adjustment to the dark. Once outside, it can take more than half an hour for your eyes to adapt fully and allow you to see faint objects.

The Perseid meteors appear to stream away from the shower's "radiant" point near the border of Perseus and Cassiopeia. (Sky & Telescope)

The meteors' radiant — the point from which they appear to originate — lies in the constellation Perseus, which gives the shower its name.

Perseus can be found low in the eastern sky after sunset and will rise higher throughout the night. But you don't have to face the constellation to see the meteors; they can streak across the entire sky.

But wait. There's more.

Two other major meteor showers are also active: the southern delta Aquariids and the alpha Capricornids.

Those showers produce far fewer meteors at their peak — about 25 and five an hour, respectively — but they still increase your chances of seeing a "shooting star."

There is also a minor shower called the kappa Cygnids, which produces about three meteors an hour at its peak.

And then there are random, or sporadic, meteors.

"So, you know, it's meteor Christmas," Brown said. "It really is."

Partial solar eclipse

Now, on to the solar eclipse.

On Aug. 12, a total solar eclipse will be visible across Greenland, Iceland and Spain, along with a very small part of Portugal.

While the total eclipse won't be visible from Canada, the moon will appear to take a small bite out of the sun.

A composite image of seven separate photographs taken with a single fixed camera shows a partial solar eclipse seen from Castillo del Romeral, on the island of Gran Canaria, Spain, March 29, 2025. Depending on your location in Canada, the Aug. 12 partial solar eclipse could look like any one of these phases. (Reuters/Borja Suarez)

The farther east you are, the bigger the bite will appear. In B.C. and Alberta, however, it will be almost imperceptible.

If you hope to see it, remember to do so carefully. Use only approved solar eclipse glasses.

"If you have the appropriate solar filters available, watching the sun be 'eaten' by the moon is very neat!" said Paul Delaney, an astronomer and professor emeritus in York University 's department of physics and astronomy in Toronto.

A solar eclipse is a great way to see celestial motion of the Earth, moon and sun in action, he said.

"Almost humbling in my opinion."

World.title: Trump was shuttled between planes in a catering truck during NATO trip as a ruse, major U.S. papers report
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President ​Donald Trump took a secret military flight from Turkey last month in an operation that involved him being moved between aircraft in a catering truck, a deception prompted by an Iranian assassination threat, the Washington Post reported.

The White House said at the time that the president was flying aboard Air Force One from Turkey, where he had attended a NATO summit, to Britain. But moments ‌after Trump boarded the plane, he left it in secret via the catering truck and boarded another aircraft for the flight to Britain, the Post said on Monday, quoting unnamed sources.

The New York Times carried a similar report, quoting unnamed U.S. officials.

Trump had taken a newly renovated Qatari-donated jet to Ankara for the NATO summit but unexpectedly announced he would use an older Air Force One when ​departing the country, a move that prompted questions about the newer plane's security.

The trip to ​NATO was the first international travel for the new plane, whose speedy upgrades triggered questions over its cost and security, and took place as hostilities escalated with Iran, which borders Turkey.

Before departing Ankara, Trump said on Truth Social that he would use ​an older baby blue Air Force One plane "for old time's sake" to RAF Mildenhall in Britain while the new ⁠plane stopped at the same base so ⁠U.S. service members stationed there could tour the aircraft.

WATCH | Seeing a threat to press freedom: 'Aggressive' subpoenas on New York Times journalists part of a larger pattern, says advocate | Duration 5:39 The New York Times says the U.S. Department of Justice ordered several of its journalists to testify before a grand jury following their coverage of security concerns regarding President Donald Trump's Qatari-donated Air Force One. Gabe Rottman with the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press explains why he thinks it threatens press freedom.

Questions about Qatari-donated plane

The deception operation was triggered by a credible threat to Trump, the Post reported. A similar operation took place in 2000, when President Bill Clinton ⁠used an unmarked executive jet to fly into Pakistan while sending his formal Air Force One as a decoy.

On this occasion, the journalists who thought they were travelling with Trump on the older Air Force One, which was effectively used as a decoy, reported being advised to keep their window shades in the press cabin closed. The ‌Post said aside from reporters, some White House staff also believed that the president was on board.

Trump, right, gives the peace sign to members of the media after arriving on July 8 in Suffolk, England, with military members and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, second from right, standing nearby. (Jonathan Ernst/Reuters)

When asked later by reporters why they had to keep their shades shut during the flight, Trump said it was because they were "probably on a dangerous flight." He went on to say: “But if I go, you go. Right?"

The C-32A carrying Trump flew to Britain and arrived at around 10:20 p.m. with the older Air ​Force One and media arriving minutes later, the Post reported. It was not clear, the paper said, how Trump was moved from the C-32A back to the older Air Force One.

After Trump climbed down the stairs of the older Air Force One, he gave the media a peace sign but didn't walk over to ⁠talk to them. He then spent some time greeting service members before walking to the new, Qatar-donated plane.

When asked for comment on the revelation ⁠of a ⁠secret flight on a third plane, the White House provided ​a statement from communications director Steve Cheung saying the Qatari-donated jet has been fitted with high-level security protocols that ensure the safety of the president and his ​staff.

"As the president has said recently, there are ⁠many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats," Cheung said. It was the same statement provided to the Post.

The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The new plane, with red, white, dark blue and gold livery chosen by Trump, is a Boeing 747 gifted to the United States by Qatar last year and refitted by defence contractor L3Harris Technologies. It was intended to serve as a temporary replacement ⁠while Boeing struggled to deliver long-delayed next-generation Air Force ‌One planes.

Since a U.S. airstrike on Baghdad in 2020 killed high-profile Iranian military leader Qassem Soleimani, American intelligence and law enforcement agencies have tracked multiple alleged plots linked to Iranian individuals targeting Trump, officials in his first presidential administration and other individuals in the U.S.

World.title: The World Cup can make a country famous. Can it make people visit?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

You might have tuned in to watch Norway play soccer. Now you’re Googling the fjords.

That’s the kind of curiosity travel companies say the World Cup can create — turning a country people may know little about into a place they want to see for themselves.

For Marc Sison, the vice-president of Central and Northern Europe at tour operator Goway Travel, Norway kept coming up in conversations with clients as the tournament unfolded.

Some were drawn to the country’s Viking history and imagery, he says. Others wanted to experience the culture they had caught glimpses of while watching the team play.

“We thought the World Cup enlightened a lot of our clients that might not ever have heard of some of these destinations,” said Sison, who is based in Toronto.

Traditional travel campaigns can spend months — and plenty of money — selling a destination’s landmarks, food and scenery. But the World Cup lets millions of people get acquainted with lesser known countries like Norway, Cape Verde or Morocco and their people in real time.

Fans cheer as Norway's forward Erling Braut Haaland is seen on the screen after the victory in 2026 World Cup round of 32 football match between Ivory Coast and Norway. (Javad Parsa/NTB/AFP via Getty Images)

On the website for travel agency Nordic Visitor, traffic to its Norway destination pages jumped to "roughly double" normal levels on the two days Norway played its knockout matches, says Willow Wood, digital public relations lead based in Scotland.

She says the spikes came during Norway’s match against Brazil on July 5 and its quarter-final against England on July 11.

“The country had a spotlight on it [that] money simply can't buy,” said Wood. “It's genuinely hard to untangle how much is the performance, how much is Erling Haaland, and how much is the broader appetite for Nordic travel, but the attention itself is undeniable.”

For Sison, that human connection is what makes the tournament such a powerful showcase.

“I think that's why Norway won a lot of hearts, right? The way they showed up in the field was so inspiring being an underdog.”

Airbnb also saw searches for accommodation in Norway increase by 15 per cent between June 11 and July 12 compared with the same period in 2025, according to a spokesperson.

And some travel companies say the interest has already translated into bookings.

Anders Lindström, head of public relations and communications for Hurtigruten, a Norwegian cruise company, says bookings made by Canadians using their website increased by 110 per cent over normal levels during the World Cup.

Hurtigruten, a Norwegian cruise line, says they saw a 110 per cent increase in bookings by Canadian tourists. (Hurtigruten/Stian Klo)

What it’s meant for Norway

The boost in interest brought on by the World Cup “feels great,” said Aase Marthe J. Horrigmo, director of Visit Norway, the country’s official travel guide operated by the Norwegian government’s national tourism board.

But Horrigmo, who is based in Norway, says the challenge is turning the attention into an actual trip. When Visit Norway sees someone showing interest in the country through social media or Google searches, its team can target them with more Norway-focused articles, films and campaigns — something its social media team has been doing throughout the summer.

“Nothing happens if you don’t work hard for it,” she said. “We have the attention at the moment [and] we need to work to keep the attention.”

Horrigmo adds that travel agents, local businesses and activity providers all have a role to play, ensuring there’s enough infrastructure to support more visitors, from flights and hotel rooms to services on the ground.

From left to right: The Oseberg Ship at the Viking Ship Museum in Bygdøy, Norway; Aase Marthe J. Horrigmo is the director of Visit Norway; Kunstsilo Museum showcases art collections and digital art experiences in Kristiansand, Norway. (Johan Berge/Visit Norway, Siri-Ann Roska/Innovation Norway, Alan Williams Photography/Visit Norway)

And she says they want to draw travellers throughout the year to ease overcrowding during the summer and help protect the environment, because the goal isn’t simply to bring in as many tourists as possible.

“We have a Norwegian saying: ‘You shouldn’t saw off the branch you’re sitting on’ so we need to make sure that we take good care of the nature,” said Horrigmo.

Though Norway is best known for its fjords and mountains, Horrigmo says she wants travellers to see a more nuanced view of the country, including its modern cities, alongside a cultural identity rooted in its Viking heritage and the traditions of the Sámi, the Indigenous people of the Scandinavian Arctic.

“This World Cup … has been very good for Norway as a destination,” said Horrigmo.

For sustainable tourism, Horrigmo wants to encourage people to visit Norway year-round, rather than concentrating their trips in the summer. (Ruben Soltvedt/Visit Norway)

Other countries have experienced the same

Cape Verde, known officially as the Republic of Cabo Verde, is a group of islands off the west coast of Africa that has flown under the radar for many international travellers, and also found itself the subject of curiosity during this World Cup.

Its inspiring run prompted more people to ask where the country was — and how they could visit, according to Christian Wolters, the president of Intrepid Canada.

For travel companies, Wolters says, major sporting events can offer travel companies a glimpse into places that people are suddenly eager to explore more about.

“I know a few of our internal employees were excited to say, “Hey, could we put Cape Verde into our [offerings]?” said Wolters.

“[The World Cup] is a great way to step through the looking glass of social media where you're actually meeting human beings and you get to really learn about who they are, what their country is all about, and their culture.”

From left to right: The agricultural city of Assomada in Santiago, Cape Verde; friends play soccer at a beach; Praia city in Cape Verde. (John Wessels/AFP via Getty Images, Patrick Meinhardt/AFP via Getty Images, John Wesselss/AFP via Getty Images)

At the World Cup in 2022, the tournament also helped fuel interest in Morocco following the historic success of its team, which finished fourth.

“The growth of the Moroccan soccer team has brought a lot of curiosity,” said Christa Kucey, the Honorary Consul of the Kingdom of Morocco for B.C. based in Vancouver.

“People are like, ‘Who are these? How did this happen? Where are they from?”

From left to right: Kasbah des Caid in Tamnoulgat, Morocco; women dressed in traditional clothing in Morocco's southern Sahara desert; Grand Theatre of Rabat in Rabat, Morocco. (Raj Alaya/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images, Abdelmajid Bziouat/AFP via Getty Images)

Morocco has become Africa’s most visited country, welcoming 17.4 million visitors in 2024 and a record 19.8 million in 2025. Kucey says the World Cup may have helped drive that growth, and with Morocco set to co-host the World Cup in 2030, she expects visitor numbers to continue climbing.

“I think the World Cup opened the door for people to get more curious and want to explore more about Morocco, but it’s when people go and experience the people, their hospitality that keep people going back,” said Kucey.

World.title: Paul St-Pierre Plamondon: Anglo-Quebecers deserve better government
World.content:
Article content

We must state it plainly and without hesitation: we’ve gone through one of the worst regressions in quality of life in Quebec’s recent history. Quebecers know it, and they see it in their daily lives. Their purchasing power has vanished, home ownership has become an increasingly distant dream for too many young people. Our health-care and education systems are struggling to provide the quality of services that our citizens have every right to expect. Security and tidiness have suddenly become major issues in our cities and the number of homeless people has exploded. Meanwhile, our infrastructure projects make headlines only because of soaring costs and endless delays. While the government neglected road maintenance, schools and hospitals, it has normalized the waste of public funds through scandals like SAAQclic and financial debacles such as Northvolt. A part of that decline is connected to the ideological beliefs at the federal level that brought uncontrolled and unlimited immigration during those eight years, yet the Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) chose to stand by as a resigned spectator, leading to the consequences we see today.

World.title: West Colombia earthquake killed more than 227 people, say local authorities
World.content:
Local and regional authorities have said that at least 227 people were confirmed killed in Monday’s earthquake while search and rescue teams continue to look for survivors.

So far, 120 people were confirmed dead in Valle del Cauca where locals said that entire towns in the north of the province were all but destroyed by the 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck the Choco province on Monday.

In Cali, the capital of Valle del Cauca, rescue workers continued to look for survivors under the rubble of apartment buildings that collapsed. Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder imposed a curfew in the city after locals chased him away from a search and rescue operation.

Choco Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said that mayors from the capital Quibdo and 22 affected towns reported 14 deaths and 140 injuries.

Multiple parts of the western province have yet to be contacted, however, as the local energy and telephone grid were destroyed by the earthquake, said Cordoba.

In Pereira, a city located at only 60 kilometers of the earthquake’s epicenter, and the surrounding Risaralda province, at least 88 people had died and dozens were still missing.

All major cities in the coffee region, Choco and Valle del Cauca declared an emergency to deal with the hundreds of injured that required medical attention at one of the cities’ hospitals.

President Abelardo de la Espriella said Tuesday morning that the earthquake destroyed more than 5,000 homes and that 188 people were missing.

The National Army and fire brigades from across Colombia sent teams to the cities in the disaster area to help with local search and rescue missions.

The US Department of State said it had committed $15.5 million “in funding for emergency shelter, food, protection, and earthquake assessments” for Colombia.

The Chinese embassy in Bogota said that Chinese companies that operate in Colombia were “sending heavy equipment to the most affected areas of the earthquake, participating in rescue efforts and the clearing of debris, in order to rescue the affected population using all available means.”

World.title: Colombia declares national disaster after devastating earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella declared a national disaster and sent his ministers to the west of Colombia to coordinate rescue operations in response to a 7.4M earthquake.

Following an emergency meeting at disaster management agency UNGRD, De la Espriella said he would travel to Pereira, one of the worst hit cities, to further coordinate the government response.

Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara would coordinate rescue operations for the rest of the coffee region, the health and defense ministers would travel to the Choco and Transport Minister Elsa Noguera would coordinate efforts in Valle del Cauca from Cali.

De la Espriella canceled plans he had to visit La Guajira, a northern province that wasn’t affected by the earthquake.

Throughout the morning, local and regional media reported dozens of collapsed buildings in multiple cities in Valle del Cauca, the coffee region and Choco.

More than 110 people were killed and dozens were injured because of the earthquake, De la Espriella said at a press conference.

The earthquake damaged more than 1,500 homes and destroyed 37. Sixty-one buildings collapsed and 18 healthcare centers suffered damage as well as 52 schools and 17 community centers.

The roof of the Pereira airport also came down and five other airports in western Colombia reported damages, said the president.

According to the National Police, road travel has been complicated because of landslides and fallen trees.

The government has yet to report on missing persons.

“Right now, the most important thing is to protect lives, rescue those who remain trapped, treat the injured, and bring aid to the hardest-hit communities,” said Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo.

“United we will overcome this emergency,” Restrepo added.

The vice-president, together with Foreign Minister Omar Bula, will coordinate foreign aid.

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade and the strongest in the west of the country since 1979.

World.title: 7.4M earthquake hits western Colombia: at least 110 killed, dozens of buildings collapsed
World.content:
An M7.4 earthquake hit western Colombia on Monday, killing at least 110 people and injuring hundreds.

The earthquake struck around 7:30 and had its epicenter in San Jose del Palmar, a municipality in the Choco province.

In the hour that followed, locals began reporting collapsed buildings in the cities of Cali, Pereira and Manizales, where a tower of the cathedral and a dozen other buildings fully or partially collapsed, according to Mayor Jorge Eduardo Rojas.

In a first report on fatalities, Risaralda Governor Juan Diego Patiño said that at least 40 people were killed in the capital Perira. Another three would have been killed in Manizales.

In Cali, an unknown number of people would be trapped under the rubble of multiple buildings. At least 27 people would be killed in the Valle del Cauca province.

Large parts of the roof of the Pereira airport came down, according to video shared on social media.

Flights to Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura were suspended while airport authorities check for damages to infrastructure

In Quibdo, the capital of Choco, at least four people were killed and another 69 were injured, Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said in her second report.

The earthquake was also felt strongly in the capital Bogota and in Medellin where no injuries were reported.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said on social media platform X that he had “personally taken charge of the emergency response in San José del Palmar.”

“I will also be in Pereira in person to stand with those affected and monitor the government’s response,” said De la Espriella, who took office on Friday and has yet to appoint his director of disaster response agency UNGRD.

The president later reported that he was on his way to Bogota to lead rescue efforts from the UNGRD’s main office.

I have established a Unified Command Post at the UNGRD, from where I will personally lead the efforts to assist the communities in Chocó, the Coffee Region, and all affected areas. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade.

World.title: US seeks $1B aid package for Colombia’s new government
World.content:
Th US State Department said it will ask Congress for $1 billion for “deepening our shared and economic partnership” with the government of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

The funding boost, which resembles that of the first year of Plan Colombia in 2000, seeks to “support the De la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten US, Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity.”

In preliminary talks, De la Espriella had already agreed to join the “Shield of the Americas,” a regional initiative of far-right governments to jointly fight crime.

According to a fact sheet, the funds that would require congressional approval would be used to:

Strengthen Colombia’s security forces

Disrupt illegal armed groups and organized crime’s ability to launder money

Significantly expand coca eradication and cocaine interdiction operations

Halt migration

Increase State presence in conflict regions

Combat child recruitment and exploitation by illegal armed groups

The administration of President Donald Trump also seeks to “increase trade and deepen economic ties between our countries.”

In order to do this, nominated US ambassador Nate Morris told the Senate that De la Espriella would withdraw from a memorandum of understanding with the government of China that sought to improve ties with the Asian giant.

Trump’s aid package would help Colombian communities “recover from potential El Niño-related flooding, drought,” which is expected to cause emergencies between December and March.

The US would also support a Bilateral Prosperity Dialogue to “stabilize” Colombia’s economy, “strengthening its energy generation and distribution sectors, exploring critical mineral investments, and creating new opportunities for US investors.”

The aid package would additionally “strengthen Colombian small and medium enterprises in agribusiness, manufacturing, and tech services by connecting them to US buyers and linking them to U.S.-aligned supply chains.”

The two governments would additionally seek to modernize Colombia’s digital, port and energy infrastructure while “positioning Colombia as a trusted nearshoring partner for supply chain diversification.”

World.title: De la Espriella sworn in as Colombia’s new president
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in in Colombia’s third largest city, Cali, under extreme security precautions.

De la Espriella was sworn in by the president of Congress, Senator Honorio Henriquez of the far-right Democratic Center party in the theater of the private University of Santiago de Cali.

The first part of the ceremony was attended by the Spanish King Felipe VI, multiple heads of state from Latin America and more than 60 ambassadors.

After being sworn in, De la Espriella went to the nearby Pichincha Battalion to assume the supreme command of the armed forces and hold his first speech as president.

The president vowed the security forces that he would be “an essential part of the miracle country” and vowed that at the end of his four-year mandate “authority will be felt in every corner of the country.”

De la Espriella also promised that “nobody will be persecuted for his opinions” and warned members of the “regime” of former President Gustavo Petro he would cooperate with “other States,” suggesting they could be extradited.

Both ceremonies were boycotted by Petro’s leftist political party, the Historic Pact, which organized political rallies elsewhere in Cali, and in the cities of Bogota and Barranquilla.

In Barranquilla, Senator Ivan Cepeda stressed the left does not recognize the incoming government because of De la Espriella’s US citizenship and his alleged debts with the US Department of Justice.

“De la Espriella, who once acted as an intermediary for drug traffickers and paramilitaries—from whose ill-gotten gains he has profited—has now become a figure who will be pressured by the United States, by his own government, and by its federal agencies to allow all kinds of foreign intervention in Colombia,” said Cepeda.

The leftist senator lost the elections to De la Espriella with a razor-thin margin of less than one percent. His supporters continue to seek a court order to nullify the election.

World.title: Colombia investigating governors, mayors over $941M corruption racket
World.content:
Prosecutors arrested 13 suspects and asked Colombia’s Supreme Court to investigate seven (former) governors over their alleged involvement in the embezzlement of COP3 trillion ($941 million).

The arrests and the investigation requests are related to the public-private partnership Sierra Nevada Mixed Fund, which was created by Martin Zuleta (U Party) and his family when he was mayor of La Paz, Cesar, in early 2021.

While supposedly serving the interests of La Paz, the Sierra Nevada Mixed Fund allegedly used forged documents to illegally appropriate funds from the General Royalties System with the help of governors from at least five provinces.

“So far, we’ve tracked 3 trillion pesos, of which it has been established that some were misappropriated through irregular contracts,” anti-corruption prosecutor Madeleyne Perez said at a press conference.

Among those whose cases were forwarded to the Supreme Court were the governors of Magdalena, Vichada, Amazonas Guaviare an Vaupes.

Former Governors Rafael Martinez of Magdalena and Alvaro Leon of Vichada will also be investigated by the Supreme Court.

Among those who were arrested is the mayor of Maria la Baja, a contractor and multiple (former) directors of the mixed fund.

The non-profit has been investigated since 2024 when authorities found irregularities in the construction of a high school in the Huila province, funds for school transport in Casanare and funds meant for indigenous reserves in La Guajira.

A report by the now-defunct radio station W from that year showed that Sierra Nevada had been hired by authorities from throughout Colombia for a wide variety of projects, avoiding any open bidding procedure.

W found more than 100 contracts between mainly local and regional government authorities and the non-profit.

According to Caracol, Zuleta was taken to hospital after his home was raided by prosecution officials and would be available to cooperate with the prosecutors investigating his alleged involvement in corruption.

World.title: Colombia’s left presents evidence suggesting De la Espriella won through fraud
World.content:
Colombia’s President Gustavo Petro and data analysts presented evidence suggesting that President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella won the election through the mass manipulation of tally sheets.

During a two-hour presentation, Petro claimed that almost all tally sheets that had been shared with his political party, the Historic Pact “lacked the Hash security lock,” which is inserted into official PDF documents to guarantee they can’t be changed.

The absence of a hash file implies that the so-called E14 tally sheets may have been altered, which appears to have happened, according to data analysts who accompanied the president.

Legal expert William Villanueva said that original tally sheets were scanned and subsequently reprocessed, removing the metadata that would allow them to determine whether the E14’s were uploaded or introduced digitally.

“We found documents marked ‘confidential’… and others that said ‘not digitized’ on a blank page, which—and this is important—were later republished with different information,” said one of the computer scientists.

The investigation, which was carried out by 75,000 “digital witnesses,” found that 95 municipalities had more voters than inhabitants. In all of these municipalities, the E-14’s gave De la Espriella landslide victories with more than 70% of the votes.

The president-elect’s opponent, leftist Senator Ivan Cepeda, achieved not a single victory in hundreds of towns where the electoral census was larger than 85% of the population.

In 1,350 polling centers in capital cities, the researchers found that block patterns in which De la Espriella won the first half of the voting booths and Cepeda won the second half.

According to a consulted statistician, this result would only be probably in some 80 polling stations, said Carlos Oñoro, one of the digital witnesses.

“This order is mathematically impossible for human voters,” Petro stated, arguing that automated software replaced actual citizen ballots.

The findings of the digital witnesses will be added to a lawsuit that seeks to nullify the election of De la Espriella and force the Council of State to order a recount of the votes.

Following the presentation, Cepeda said in a post on social media network X that “the competent authority must impartially examine our demands of nullity.”

World.title: De la Espriella says he won’t allow Colombia’s left to “destabilize democracy”
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella said that he won’t allow his country’s left to “destabilize democracy” through civil disobedience against his US citizenship.

In his weekly address to the nation, De la Espriella stressed that after Friday he will be president and “with the force of the constitution and the law” ensure that his power will be upheld.

The civil disobedience announced by leftist opposition leader Ivan Cepeda “is nothing more than a euphemism for an attempt to destabilize democracy,” said De la Espriella.

“I will not allow it,” said the president-elect.

I am the president of all Colombians, and I will ensure, through the power of the Constitution and the law, that what the Colombian people decided—which was to elect me—is upheld. My call to the entire nation is that we stop normalizing what is wrong, illegal, and corrupt. Let’s call things by their proper names and confront them for what they are. This so-called “civil disobedience” is nothing more than a euphemism for an attempt to destabilize democracy, and I will not allow it. Abelardo de la Espriella

According to De la Espriella, the left “combined all forms of struggle,” a term used by the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC to justify the violence used by the insurgents, “and lost.”

Cepeda called on his followers to peaceful civil disobedience in response to the president-elect’s refusal to renounce his US citizenship.

The incoming opposition leader and his political party, the Historic Pact, support legal efforts to challenge De la Espriella’s election on claims that fraud concerns have not been tackled.

More radical elements within the Historic Pact, including outgoing President Gustavo Petro, have sustained that the far-right won the elections through deceit and fraud, but have failed to present evidence that would confirm a criminal conspiracy.

World.title: Chile’s Municipalities, Senapred Meet Ahead of Storm Forecast
World.content:
SANTIAGO, Chile â As Chile prepares for an approaching winter storm system, the Association of Municipalities of Chile (Amuch) held a high-level coordination meeting with the National Disaster Prevention and Response Service (Senapred) to strengthen municipal emergency response measures.

The discussions focused on improving collaboration among municipalities, national agencies, and private service providers to better protect residents during severe weather events.

Power Companies Face Pressure Over Response Times

A central topic in the meeting was the performance of electric utilities during past emergencies. JosÃ© Manuel Palacios, mayor of La Reina, expressed concern over delayed responses from power companies in recent years.

âWe are exploring ways, together with Senapred and other institutions, to develop more efficient actions and hold the companies accountable to meet the response times our residents need,â Palacios said.

Rural Water Supply Risks Tied to Electricity

For rural municipalities, electrical outages pose a dual threat, as potable water systems often rely on electric power. Paula GÃ¡rate, mayor of Melipilla, emphasized the heightened vulnerability of rural areas during storms.

âLosing electricity also means losing access to potable water. Many rural water systems depend on electricity, and that remains our greatest concern,â GÃ¡rate noted.

Coordinated Municipal Efforts to Mitigate Risks

Senapred Director Alicia CebriÃ¡n highlighted the essential role of municipal governments in both preparation and response phases.

âMunicipalities play a crucial role in coordination, information gathering, and implementing mitigation works to reduce the impact of winter threats on residents,â CebriÃ¡n stated.

She underscored that emergency prevention and mitigation is a shared responsibility across public agencies and institutions. âPublic authorities who are directly involved in disaster management bear this responsibility, and we are committed to fulfilling it,â she added.

Winter System Expected to Test Emergency Readiness

The coordination meeting comes as Chileâs central regions brace for a frontal system expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds. Authorities emphasized that ongoing preparation and inter-agency cooperation will be key to minimizing disruption and protecting vulnerable communities.

World.title: Brian Wilson, Legendary Beach Boys Co-Founder, Dies at 82
World.content:
LOS ANGELES â Brian Wilson, the legendary musician, songwriter and co-founder of The Beach Boys, has died at the age of 82, his family announced.

“We are heartbroken to announce that our beloved father Brian Wilson has passed away,” the family said in a statement. “We are at a loss for words right now. Please respect our privacy at this time as our family is grieving. We realize that we are sharing our grief with the world.”

Born in 1942 in Hawthorne, California, Wilson formed The Beach Boys in 1961 with his younger brothers Carl and Dennis, cousin Mike Love, and friend Al Jardine. The band became one of the most influential and commercially successful acts in music history, selling over 100 million records worldwide.

Wilson was the creative force behind the groupâs distinctive harmonies and groundbreaking studio sound. His 1966 album Pet Sounds is regarded as a masterpiece that reshaped the boundaries of pop music production.

Among The Beach Boys’ many hits, Wilson co-wrote and produced I Get Around, Help Me, Rhonda, and Good Vibrations. Rolling Stone ranked The Beach Boys 12th on its list of the “100 Greatest Artists of All Time.”

Tributes poured in following news of his death. Nancy Sinatra shared a photo with Wilson on Instagram, writing, âHis cherished music will live forever as he travels through the Universe and beyond. God bless you, sweet Brian.â

Sean Ono Lennon called Wilson the “American Mozart” and a “one of a kind genius from another world,” adding: âAnyone who really knows me knows how heartbroken I am about Brian Wilson passing. Not many people influenced me as much as he did. I feel very lucky that I was able to meet him and spend some time with him. He was always very kind and generous.”

Throughout his life, Wilson faced significant personal struggles. Diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 1984, his condition was linked by doctors to earlier psychedelic drug use. In early 2024, his family revealed he had developed dementia.

Wilson’s wife, Melinda, with whom he shared 24 years of marriage and five adopted children, died earlier in 2024. He also had two daughters, Carnie and Wendy, from his first marriage.

Despite his health battles, Wilsonâs legacy remains unparalleled. His influence on songwriting, vocal harmony, and studio innovation continues to inspire generations of musicians.

World.title: Chile and Norway Deepen Antarctic Cooperation with New Agreement
World.content:
Chile and Norway signed a memorandum of understanding on Antarctic cooperation Monday, reinforcing their shared commitment to peace, science, and environmental protection in the region.

The agreement, signed by Chilean Foreign Minister Alberto van Klaveren and Norwegian Minister of International Development Ã smund GrÃ¸ver, aims to strengthen bilateral coordination under the Antarctic Treaty System. It outlines enhanced collaboration on scientific research, climate monitoring, and the preservation of marine ecosystems through frameworks such as the Antarctic Treaty Consultative Meetings and the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR).

The accord includes provisions for regular dialogue between scientific and governmental institutions in both countries and seeks to optimize joint efforts in Antarctic and sub-Antarctic research. Both nations also pledged support for the Polar Codeâs implementation, aiming to improve safety and environmental standards for ships operating in polar waters.

Operational and logistical cooperation between Chileâs and Norwayâs national Antarctic programs will also be explored, particularly in alignment with CCAMLRâs conservation objectives.

This renewed alliance builds on the long-standing historical ties between the two nations and reaffirms their role as active stewards of one of the worldâs most fragile and strategically vital environments.

World.title: Japan Tops Global Waste Index 2025; U.S., Israel, and Chile Rank as Worst Polluters
World.content:
Japan has emerged as the world leader in waste management, while Israel, Chile, and the United States rank among the worst-performing countries, according to the Global Waste Index 2025 released by Slovak-based waste technology company Sensoneo.

The report, which ranks all 38 OECD member states based on their waste generation and disposal practices, highlights significant disparities in global waste management. Sensoneoâs index evaluates countries on per capita waste generation, recycling, incineration, and landfill use.

Israel and Chile ranked last and second-to-last, respectively, primarily due to their heavy reliance on environmentally damaging landfilling practices. Israel sends 524 of the 650 kilograms of waste it generates per person each year directly to landfills. Chile recycles just 1% of its waste and sends more than 95% to landfill.

The United States, which increased its per capita waste generation from 811 to 951 kilograms since 2022, remains the highest generator of municipal solid waste globally. The U.S. disposes of nearly half of that â 447 kilograms â in landfills annually. Neighboring Canada also performed poorly, landfilling 67% of its annual 694 kg per capita waste.

At the other end of the spectrum, Japan ranked No. 1, followed by South Korea and Estonia, all of which combine relatively low waste generation with efficient disposal methods. Japan sends only 3 kilograms per capita to landfill, relying heavily on incineration (245 kg) and maintaining a controlled recycling rate.

European countries dominated the top 10 rankings, with Austria, Germany, Finland, Belgium, Sweden, Norway, and Switzerland all demonstrating strong waste management systems. Austria topped the recycling chart with 334 kilograms of municipal waste recycled per person annually â accounting for 42% of its total waste.

Meanwhile, Spain fell four places to 27th despite minor improvements. The country reduced its landfill and incineration rates slightly while increasing recycling by 10 kilograms per capita. However, its overall waste generation rose by 10 kg compared to the 2022 index.

The index revealed that in 12 of the 38 countries, over half of all waste is still landfilled â including in developed nations like Australia, New Zealand, and Canada. By contrast, Switzerland was the only country to report zero landfill disposal, while Belgium, Finland, Estonia, and Japan landfilled less than 3 kg per person.

Other key findings include:

New Zealand , Finland , and Iceland posted the largest reductions in waste generation per capita.

, , and posted the largest reductions in waste generation per capita. From an environmental standpoint, incineration is considered preferable to landfilling, but excessive reliance on either suggests a need for stronger waste reduction and recycling strategies.

About the Index and Sensoneo

First launched in 2019, the Global Waste Index is published every three years by Sensoneo, a company specializing in digital transformation for waste management systems. The 2025 edition is based on the latest available national data.

Sensoneo operates in 87 countries and provides waste monitoring solutions to cities, industries, and governments. It is the only company to have successfully implemented deposit return systems (DRS) IT infrastructure in nine countries, achieving recycling rates above 90%.

In Madrid, Sensoneo is deploying 11,100 smart sensors, marking the worldâs largest smart waste monitoring installation to date.

World.title: South Korean Model and Actor Kim Jong Suk Dies at 29, Family Urges Respect Amid Speculation

The news has shocked fans and colleagues across the countryâs entertainment industry, where Kim rose to prominence following his appearance on tvNâs 2022 reality dating show Skip Dating.

According to the reports, law enforcement responded to the scene, after which the man allegedly died by suicide after jumping from a high-rise building.
