World.title: Germany’s modern miracle: Churches are losing believers but gaining money
World.content:
Rising salaries have outweighed the cost of hundreds of thousands leaving the church.

German commentators are calling it a modern-day “miracle.”

Hundreds of thousands of worshippers in the country are walking away from their churches each year. The money, however, keeps rolling in.

Some 660,000 people formally quit the country’s Catholic and Protestant churches in 2025, freeing them from a levy automatically charged to registered members as a percentage of their income tax bill.

Despite the exodus, the two institutions collected more than €12.5 billion through the church tax for the 2025 fiscal year, up from around €12.4 billion in 2024.

The apparent miracle has a decidedly earthly explanation: Rising wages and Germany’s progressive tax system mean the shrinking pool of members is paying more.

“At first glance, the development may seem contradictory,” a spokesperson for the Evangelical Church in Germany — the umbrella organization representing Germany’s regional Protestant churches — said. “The reason is that church tax is calculated based on individual income tax.”





Members of Germany’s Catholic and Protestant churches and some Jewish communities pay an additional religious tax equal to 8 or 9 percent of their income tax liability, even if they don’t attend services.

In 2021, the most recent year for which comprehensive data is available, more than 29 million people paid church tax in Germany, amounting to almost half of all income taxpayers in Europe’s largest economy.

The German Finance Ministry’s 2025 payroll tax tables suggests that a single employee without children earning €50,000 gross a year pays approximately €600 in church tax annually on top of income tax, depending on the federal state. Someone earning €70,000 per year pays more than €1,000.

People are registered as part of their religious community at birth or at local government offices. To stop paying the church tax, they must formally leave through a process known as Kirchenaustritt, or “church exit.”

The procedure varies across Germany’s federal states but typically requires appearing in person at a registry office or local court to submit a declaration. Most states also charge an administrative fee.

While those who deregister can still attend services as a visitor and access some church services, they are not allowed to have a church wedding, be a godparent or be guaranteed a church burial.

In 2025, some 310,000 left the Catholic Church, while around 350,000 left one of Germany’s regional Protestant churches.

Church exit

The reasons people give for formally leaving their religious communities range from feeling less connected to the church to simply wanting to save money.

“People are leaving the Church because they feel it no longer plays a role in their lives,” said Matthias Kopp, director of communications for the German Bishops’ Conference.

“Added to this are the scandals of recent years, which have called the Church’s credibility into question,” he added. “There are also people — though this is by no means the primary reason — who leave the Church because of the church tax.”

“These are processes of alienation to which we must respond,” said Kopp.

For Jana Keil, a 33-year-old accountant from Berlin, the decision was both financial and moral. “I no longer wanted to support the system with church tax in light of the [child sex] abuse scandals,” she said.





Lukas Heinich, a 23-year-old working student, said he formally left after completing his apprenticeship because he “didn’t feel like paying the tax or supporting the church.”

That church tax revenues continue to rise despite the exodus is down to the types of taxpayers choosing to remain church members.

Those who are still paying church tax in Germany are “probably the higher earners,” said Zareh Asatryan, professor of empirical economics at the University of Münster. “Those that stay will naturally earn more income because of inflation plus real wage growth, and they will just generate more revenue.”

A miracle with an end date?

But the continued rise in church tax revenue masks significant long-term challenges — and raises questions about how long the trend can last.

While those revenues are going up, they are “relatively sluggish” and “haven’t been increasing by a lot,” said Asatryan.

The increase in revenue from the church tax is considerably lower than the increase in revenue from income tax. State revenue from wage and income taxes rose by 6.65 percent in 2025, said Kopp, whereas church tax revenue increased by 1.93 percent.

“Long-term projections indicate that church tax revenue will decline significantly over the coming decades as church membership continues to decrease,” said the spokesperson for the Evangelical Church in Germany.

Protestant churches are already preparing for their income to decrease “through long-term planning processes,” said the spokesperson. “Without this system, the church’s religious, social and charitable work would not be possible on its current scale.”

World.title: EU opens channel with Meta, TikTok to tackle Ceuta migrant crisis
World.content:
That will serve as a point of contact for platforms, fact-checkers and the Commission to quickly flag content so that it can be reviewed and taken down if necessary. The effort comes amid concerns that disinformation is promoting further crossings into the territory on Aug. 15, according to Maldita.es. Maldita.es and the European Fact-Checking Standards Network attended Monday’s meeting.

The Commission operates a rapid response system under its code of conduct on disinformation, often triggered around elections. The new mechanism on Ceuta would bring a closer group of stakeholders together, two of the people said.

Another meeting has been set for later this week, one of those people and the third person confirmed.

Meta and TikTok said they were already actively monitoring the situation in line with their policies and had set up dedicated teams to monitor and respond to content in real time.

The crisis has divided EU countries and has reignited Europe’s long-running debate on illegal migration. Italy has since been one of the harshest critics of Spain’s left-wing government and its migration policies, and has implemented border controls for travelers arriving from Spain.

Former EU commissioner Thierry Breton, who was a force behind the EU’s online content rules, on Monday said the bloc should launch a disinformation inquiry into the Ceuta crisis in an interview with Italian newspaper La Stampa.

World.title: Greece’s aging power grid blamed for catastrophic wildfires
World.content:
Two deadly wildfires in late July — one in western Attica and one on the island of Crete —were also linked to the electricity grid in preliminary findings from the Greek fire brigade. The fires destroyed more than 36,000 acres and killed four people.

“Six out of 10 major fires and 55 percent of the area burnt in 2025 were caused by the power grid,” said Elias Tziritis, wildfires actions coordinator at World Wildlife Fund Greece. “Statistically speaking, the majority of fires may not start from the power grid, but these are the ones that cause the most major, devastating fires.”

Loose or sagging power lines, vegetation coming in contact with cables, dust buildup on transmission equipment and other such faults can all generate sparks. The risk rises during strong winds and periods of heavy electricity demand, when aging infrastructure is under greater strain.

Much of Greece’s electricity grid was installed decades ago and runs above ground through fire-prone forests and increasingly depopulated rural areas. In the 1960s, the country opted for an overhead network as a cheaper way to extend electricity across the country, while the prolonged financial crisis that began in 2009 further constrained investment in the system.

Critics say Greece has moved too slowly to bury distribution lines and adapt the network to increasingly severe fire conditions.

“We raised the issue years ago, calling for something to be done with the power grid urgently,” said Christos Kalogeropoulos, a retired lieutenant-general with the Fire Service and former director of the Arson Crimes unit. “We have been calling for urgent underground cabling.”

World.title: How to protect your eyes while watching the solar eclipse
World.content:
Europe is set to witness a rare celestial event on August 12, when the Moon will pass between the Earth and the Sun, casting its shadow across parts of the continent.

 

The total eclipse will be visible in Greenland, Iceland, Spain and a small area of northeastern Portugal. Other parts of Europe will experience a partial solar eclipse.

In Spain, the eclipse will cross the country from west to east before continuing over the Balearic Islands. It will be the first total solar eclipse visible from mainland Spain since 1905 and the first of three total solar eclipses that will be visible from the country between 2026 and 2028.

“This kind of eclipse happens quite often on Earth, but at different places. However, it happens in a specific place only every 400 years,” Philippe Escoubet, Space Plasma Scientist at the European Space Agency_,_ told Euronews. “So if you have an eclipse passing by your village or your city, it will not come back [for] 400 years, so it's almost a lifetime event that you want to see.”

But watching the eclipse safely requires proper eye protection.

The total eclipse will be visible in Greenland, Iceland, Spain and a small area of northeastern Portugal. Spain's National Geographic Institute

What glasses should you use?

For those who are going to watch it, eye health experts remind people to wear proper glasses, which comply with the ISO 12312-2 international safety standard.

Gabriëlle Janssen, president of the European Council of Optometry and Optics (ECOO), told Euronews that consumers should not rely solely on the ISO number printed on a product.

“The ISO number printed on the glasses does not by itself guarantee that they have been properly tested,” she said.

Janssen advised viewers to buy eclipse glasses from a reputable supplier and check them for scratches, holes or other damage before use.

The glasses should be put on before looking towards the Sun and removed only after looking away from it.

“Children should be supervised carefully,” she said.

People who do not have suitable eclipse glasses should not look directly at the Sun. Instead, they can follow the eclipse through a livestream, such as one provided by the European Southern Observatory (ESO).

Ordinary sunglasses are not a safe alternative, even if they appear very dark, as they "do not provide sufficient protection against the intense visible, ultraviolet and infrared radiation from the Sun,” Janssen said.

What about cameras, binoculars and telescopes?

Looking at the Sun through a camera, binoculars or telescope can also be dangerous unless the equipment has been fitted with a specially designed solar filter.

“Wearing eclipse glasses while looking through these devices is not sufficient, because the concentrated sunlight can damage both the filter and the eyes,” Janssen said.

Older methods sometimes suggested for viewing eclipses, including CDs and photographic negatives, should also be avoided.

“They don't block enough [light], and then some light is passing by. This can be very dangerous for your eyes,” Escoubet said.

The glasses should be put on before looking towards the Sun and removed only after looking away from it. Copyright 2024 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

Why is it important to protect the eyes?

Although the total phase of an eclipse lasts only a few minutes, looking directly at the Sun can cause permanent damage to the retina – a thin, light-sensitive layer of tissue that lines the back inner part of the eye.

Looking directly at the Sun can cause solar retinopathy, a photochemical injury to the retinal tissue. The macula, the part of the retina responsible for sharp, detailed central vision, is particularly vulnerable.

“The retina has no pain receptors. This means that the damage can occur without pain and without the person immediately realising that anything is wrong,” Janssen said, adding that symptoms often only become noticeable several hours later.

Symptoms of solar retinopathy can include blurred or reduced central vision; a dark, blurred or blind spot in the centre of the visual field; distorted vision, with straight lines appearing bent; changes in colour perception; and increased sensitivity to light.

“Anyone who notices blurred, reduced or distorted vision after looking at the Sun should avoid any further exposure and seek prompt assessment from an optometrist, ophthalmologist or other appropriate eye-care professional,” Janssen said.

While those with mild damage usually “experience gradual improvement over the following weeks or months,” full recovery “is not guaranteed,” she said.

A central blind spot, reduced visual acuity or distorted vision can persist if retinal cells are permanently damaged, she said, adding that “currently no proven treatment that can reverse solar retinal damage” exists.

“Prevention through correct eye protection is therefore essential,” she said.

World.title: EU's Taliban tension laid bare five years after Afghanistan takeover
World.content:
When news broke that members of the Taliban visited Brussels in late June to discuss migration with European Union officials, Sami Samar said she was left crestfallen.

 

“I was so disappointed because we really count on European countries as they believe the principle of human rights and the universality of human rights,” she tells Euronews.

“This is kind of (an) endorsement of the Taliban, even if it's low rank of the Taliban.”

Samar, a former Afghan minister for women’s affairs from 2001 to 2002 turned human rights advocate living in exile in the United States, made the comments in the days leading up to 15 August 2026.

This is five years since the Taliban established itself as the de facto government of Afghanistan, which only Russia formally recognises. This date also marks the beginning of when the US withdrew its troops from the landlocked South Asian country after maintaining a presence there for nearly 20 years.

In the half-decade since this date, the country plunged into crisis.

The International Committee of the Red Cross says Afghanistan’s humanitarian situation remains among the most severe in the world.

Taliban fighters and supporters ride on a pickup truck during celebrations marking the anniversary of the US withdrawal in Kabul, 15 August, 2025 AP Photo

The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs estimates roughly 21.9 million people (45% of the total population) are projected to require humanitarian assistance in 2026.

This is due to years of armed conflict, economic fragility, underinvestment in basic services and the rapid attrition of rights.

Women and girls

Samar said life has deteriorated in Afghanistan as the Taliban’s grip on power has tightened.

“It’s a human rights disaster,” she said, adding that women and girls are particularly impacted with more than 160 decrees issued "reducing” their lives.

This includes banning girls from education beyond sixth grade, banning women from university and excluding women from most workplaces. It also spans imposing strict dress codes and restricting women and girls from travelling without a male guardian.

Human Rights Watch states these policies amount to crimes against humanity through gender persecution.

“They are putting more restrictions on women's freedom and movement, and violating women's rights, including women's voice should not be heard. Can you imagine that you cannot even cry loudly?” Samar said.

Afghan girls hold an illegal protest to demand the right to education in a private home in Kabul, Afghanistan, 2 August, 2022. AP

A majority of members of the European Parliament in May condemned the restrictions of the rights of girls, women and other minorities in the country, as well as public floggings and executions.

The MEPs also called on the European Commission and member states to maintain non-recognition and non-normalisation of the Taliban regime, while also laying bare their “regret” the decision to invite the Taliban to the Belgian capital.

European Commission spokesperson Anitta Hipper said on Tuesday the EU remains “gravely concerned” about systematic human rights violations in Afghanistan five-years on from the Taliban sweeping Kabul and a mantle of authority.

“The EU continues to call on the Afghan de facto authorities to respect, protect and fulfil the human rights and freedoms of all Afghans and to abide by Afghanistan's international obligation,” she said.

Hipper said member states in 2021 mandated that the EU executive maintain “operational engagement” with the de facto Afghan authorities.

“That being said, we do not recognise such or legitimise the authorities, but we speak with Taliban on topics that we consider our key values and interests,” she added.

These benchmarks span the condemnation of human rights violations in Afghanistan — such as gender-based discrimination — and standing ready to adopt targeted restrictive measures against those responsible for these violations and abuses.

Samar said these comments, which come months after earlier talks with European Commission officials and members of the Taliban on European soil, reveal a “double standard” by the bloc.

“There is a slight, very light condemnation of the situation of human rights in Afghanistan, but then you receive their delegation quietly?” she said.

“How can we trust these partnerships?”

A classroom that previously was used for girls sits empty in Kabul, 22 December, 2022 AP

Meeting about migration

The closed-door migration talks were conducted by officials from the European Commission and 15 member states as well as a delegation of Taliban representatives on 23 June. They occurred off official EU premises.

The Taliban stated the technical talks concerned the return of Afghan nationals without a right to stay in Europe, while the European Commission stressed it was about expediting returns involving people convicted of serious crimes or considered security threats.

Despite the scope, it drew fierce condemnation. UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk told Euronews he was concerned about Afghan nationals being deported into a situation where “they may be tortured.”

Swedish Migration Minister Johan Forssell told local media, however, that it is “incredibly important” these individuals are deported.

A Taliban fighter stands on a hill overlooking a camp housing Afghan refugees in Torkham, 31 May, 2025 AP Photo

"And that is not possible today. They do not want to participate. They do not want to go home,” he said.

In Sweden, roughly 200 Afghan nationals are awaiting deportation having been convicted of serious crimes, such as aggravated rape and aggravated drug trafficking, Forssell explained.

Amid the criticism, he argued that his government must negotiate with dictatorships in certain situations to "protect Swedish interests."

Deportations have proven particularly difficult for Afghans, who were among the top nationalities served with return orders in 2025.

According to Eurostat, out of the 14,270 Afghan nationals ordered to leave the bloc in the first nine months of last year, only 340 were sent back, representing a 2% return rate.

Meanwhile, arrivals into Europe continue.

Migrants walk under a railway bridge in the town of Flen, roughly 100 kilometres west of Stockholm, Sweden, 30 August, 2018. AP

More than 3,300 Afghans irregularly crossed EU borders in the first four months of 2026, mostly through the Eastern Mediterranean route, and over 63,000 Afghan nationals sought asylum in the EU in 2025, 10% of the overall number of asylum seekers.

According to Samar, these individuals are illegally entering the EU as the legal pathways to obtain a visa are onerous and because remaining in Afghanistan is perilous.

“Because of the dire situation that they face in Afghanistan, they try to cross the border," she said.

World.title: UK set to record 'warmest summer on record' as Europe preps for yet another heatwave
World.content:
The United Kingdom is on course to record its "warmest summer on record," according to the country's national weather service.

 

Provisional statistics released by the Met Office on Tuesday showed that the current recorded mean temperature across the UK from 1 June to 10 August was 16.48°C - 1.88°C above the average for 1991-2020.

"To equal the current UK summer mean temperature record of 16.12°C set in 2025, the remainder of August would only need to average 0.21°C below the 1991-2020 long-term average for meteorological summer," the Met Office said. "Any warmer than this would establish a new UK record, with records starting in 1884".

In England, the mean summer temperature has so far clocked in at 18.19°C over the same period - up 2.46°C on the average - meaning the rest of the month would need to be 1.41°C below the nation's summer average to equal the current record, which was also set in 2025, per the Met Office.

A record-breaking summer is also looking likely in Wales, which has recorded a mean summer temperature of 16.8°C so far, 2.17°C above average.

Mike Kendon, a senior scientist with the Met Office, said: "Another record-breaking summer now looks increasingly likely for the UK, following the second-warmest June, and second-warmest July on record and yet another heatwave imminent."

"These statistics are a clear reminder – if one were needed – of the stark changes that we are seeing in the UK’s climate," he added.

It comes as the Met Office issued amber heat alerts for parts of the UK on Thursday, with temperatures expected to reach up to 37°C in some areas.

Western Europe is also gearing up to face yet another heatwave this week.

In France, 43 departments are under an orange heat alert on Tuesday. That number will rise to 78 on Wednesday as the heat intensifies, with temperatures of up to 40°C forecast.

Much of Spain is also facing weather warnings, with sweltering conditions potentially exceeding 40°C in parts of the country.

The brutal weather has put increasing strain on emergency services across the continent in recent months, while also helping the spread of a series of deadly wildfires and severe droughts.

There has also been an uptick in excess deaths linked to the heatwaves. In England, a report by the UK Health Security Agency showed there were 2,877 excess deaths caused by heatwaves in May and June.

World.title: EU coordinates fact-checkers with Meta and TikTok to avoid another online-fuelled Ceuta crisis
World.content:
TikTok and Meta have agreed to join a voluntary coordination mechanism chaired by the European Commission with fact-checkers, following the spread of disinformation online that fuelled the mass crossings in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, in which around 100 people died.

 

On Monday, Henna Virkkunen, the European Commission's Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, announced that TikTok and Meta had activated a crisis protocol to set up a cooperation mechanism with fact-checkers after tens of thousands of migrants illegally crossed the Spanish border.

"The EU Commission, Europol and platforms are exchanging daily and we have increased our coordination," Virkkunen wrote on X. "TikTok and Meta have activated crisis protocols and have now put in place an ad-hoc escalation and cooperation mechanism with fact-checkers."

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said in a national television address at the peak of the influx that human traffickers had deliberately manipulated the interpretation of a recent Spanish Supreme Court ruling, which found that migrants who entered by sea could not be immediately pushed back across the border.

"What has emerged from our talks with Moroccan authorities is that trafficking mafias took a self-serving interpretation of a Supreme Court ruling," he said. That interpretation "spread like wildfire in recent hours."

Fact-checking platform Maldita confirmed that messages falsely claiming asylum would be granted to anyone entering Ceuta and Melilla circulated on social media, encouraging people to cross the border illegally.

In a letter European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen sent to Sánchez following the mass crossing, she set out a five-point plan to prevent future incidents, including an early-warning system that also covers social media activity.

"We continue to be vigilant in our work with our agencies and the platforms to stifle criminal networks selling false premises at the cost of lives," Commission spokesperson Balazs Ujvari said on Tuesday.

The crisis protocol was activated under the EU's code of conduct on disinformation, a voluntary tool that online platforms can use to comply with the bloc's rulebook for online services, the Digital Services Act (DSA).

Meta and TikTok committed to working with fact-checkers after a meeting organised by the Commission on Friday, during which the parties agreed to establish an ad hoc cooperation mechanism.

"Through this mechanism, the platforms get better information from the fact-checkers — like any harmful disinformation related to, for example, a potential new mass crossing of the border — and on that basis the platforms can take action," Ujvari added.

Because the mechanism is voluntary, it has allowed the Commission to nudge platforms to moderate the content they host, even outside the EU, where Brussels normally has no jurisdiction to enforce the DSA or other rules.

For the Commission, the advantage of working with fact-checkers is their command of local context, knowledge that can help streamline the platforms' moderation efforts, since all parties have committed to prohibiting smuggling-related content.

A TikTok spokesperson told Euronews that the company had activated a task force in response to the situation in Ceuta, setting up a team to closely monitor regional trends and mitigate emerging threats in real time, including potential deceptive behaviour.

“We have a team monitoring the situation in Ceuta in real time and removing content that violates our policies - including content that offers to provide, facilitate or seek human smuggling services," a Meta spokesperson told Euronews.

World.title: This new hotel booking platform promises VIP perks without the usual loyalty scheme faff
World.content:
Luxury hotel perks have long been a bit of a complex game.

 

You’ve traditionally had to have to be a member of the right loyalty scheme, hold a certain credit card or jump through all numbers of hoops.

Now, though, a new booking platform is promising to make VIP treatment much easier to access. Travel Habit is launching with access to more than 2,300 luxury hotels, bundling perks including room upgrades, breakfast, hotel credits and late check-outs into a single membership.

The platform will unite some of the world’s best and strongest hospitality status memberships and VIP travel networks.

The likes of Virtuoso, Ritz Carlton STARS, Rosewood Elite, Marriott STARS & Luminous, Four Seasons Preferred, Hyatt Privé, Buckingham and Lloyd's will be assembled into a single, automated booking platform.

The idea is to make life easier for guests who previously spent their time chasing perks from room upgrades to priority check-in.

The platform will do away with the necessity to be loyal to an individual hotel group, pay high annual fees on credit cards, or navigate multiple high-end VIP travel advisors.

What are the benefits?

Travel Habit members will benefit from a streamlined process and, the company says, early members are already receiving at least $7,000 (€6,055) in privileges each year, across a worldwide collection of some 2,300 luxury hotels and resorts.

The platform has been tested for the last two years on elite business and luxury travellers to ensure clients get the best value possible.

“So many clients told me their elite credit card promised upgrades they rarely actually received,” Amanda Archer, founder and CEO of Travel Habit, said.

“Our mission is to provide instant VIP access for all of our members, elevating every hotel and resort stay with world-class service and exclusive benefits members can count on,” she added.

Members keen to take advantage of the service will be able to access perks including complimentary breakfast for two, welcome notes, the highest priority room upgrades – subject to availability upon check-in – and early check-in and late check-out privileges, whenever it’s available.

World.title: Italy’s Po river runs low as drought threatens farms and water supplies
World.content:
At the confluence with the Ticino, boats now sit in shallow, muddy water surrounded by sand, algae and exposed gravel banks. The Po River Basin Authority says flows are well below seasonal averages, with levels at several monitoring stations approaching or exceeding records set during the severe drought of 2022.

 

The Po is vital to northern Italy’s agricultural heartland, including the Food Valley around Parma, where fruit, vegetables and rice depend on its water. Exceptionally low levels are also affecting supplies, with Ansa reporting tanker deliveries to more than 100 municipalities in Piedmont and Lombardy.

Around Pavia, the river has narrowed to a shallow channel, leaving large areas of riverbed exposed and making navigation increasingly difficult for leisure boats and rowing clubs. In the rice-growing Lomellina area, officials warn that the situation could worsen without significant rainfall, forcing farmers to rely increasingly on groundwater and emergency measures.

Further downstream, near Parma, tributaries and irrigation canals serving intensive fruit and vegetable farming are also running low. Farmers report that water rationing is already affecting irrigation schedules, while the basin authority has identified the stretch below Piacenza as particularly vulnerable as falling water levels expose tree trunks and other debris.

In Turin, the Po has been reduced to a slow-moving, algae-covered channel. Municipal crews have been using excavators mounted on barges to clear dense growth of invasive aquatic plants near the city centre. Regional data show that the river’s flow through Turin has fallen by more than half since June, while at the Sant’Antonio island monitoring station downstream, discharge has at times dropped to around a quarter of its normal level.

Officials warn that heat and low water are accelerating algae and invasive species, disrupting navigation and recreation. The prolonged heat has also worsened drought and wildfires across Europe, putting further pressure on water resources.

World.title: Hungary's parliament approves Orbán-critic and former judge András Baka as president
World.content:
Hungarian lawmakers approved former supreme court chief András Baka as the country's new president on Tuesday following the contested removal last month of the previous head of state as pro-EU conservative Prime Minister Péter Magyar pushes to loosen his predecessor's lingering hold over state institutions.

 

Parliament, where the ruling Tisza party holds a two-thirds majority, elected Baka, who served 17 years as a judge on the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR), with 140 votes in favour and six votes against.

Tisza nominated 73-year-old Baka for the largely ceremonial role on Saturday.

Magyar said Baka's life served "as an example of commitment to the democratic rule of law and constitutional principles" as the central European country needs to be "guided back onto the path of the rule of law and constitutional governance."

President-elect András Baka receives congratulations from Prime Minister Péter Magyar after being elected President of the Republic in Budapest, 11 August, 2026 AP Photo

'Captured state'

Hungary's previous president, Tamás Sulyok, saw his mandate cut short by a constitutional amendment, adopted as part of Magyar's reform push.

Magyar's party won elections in April by a landslide, ending nationalist Viktor Orbán's 16 years in power and promising "system change."

But rights watchdogs criticised Sulyok's removal, comparing the tinkering to the methods Orbán used to build his self-styled "illiberal" system.

Orbán's Fidesz party, along with its ally KDNP, boycotted the parliamentary vote, arguing Sulyok's ouster was "tyrannical" and "illegitimate."

Fidesz party head and former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán speaks to the press in Budapest, 13 June, 2026 AP Photo

Baka has not been critical of Sulyok's removal, despite the fact he was terminated with a similar legislative act.

"In a country governed by the rule of law, such extraordinary measures cannot be used, but Hungary became a captured state under Orbán," he told the AFP news agency last month.

State officials like the president "were appointed not to restrain the government's power, but to ensure the political survival of the former system even after an electoral defeat," Baka added.

'Restoration of liberal democracy'

Installing Baka as president signals a "guarantee that the restoration of liberal democracy will proceed along a clearly defined path," Bulcsu Zsiga, from the Centre for Fair Political Analysis, told AFP.

Besides a brief stint as a lawmaker, elected from the conservative Hungarian Democratic Forum's (MDF) party list in 1990, after the democratic transition, Baka did not hold any political positions.

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar speaks at a press conference in Budapest, 30 July, 2026 AP Photo

He was a judge at the Strasbourg-based European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) from 1991-2008.

In 2009, he was nominated as the head of the Supreme Court, but was ousted in 2012 after he condemned a move under Orbán to reduce the age of mandatory retirement for judges from 70 to 62, calling it a judicial purge.

The European Union and the United States both called the age-limit reduction illegal and in 2016 the ECHR ruled that Baka's dismissal amounted to a violation of his freedom of expression.

"His nomination also carries a symbolic meaning, given that Baka went all the way to prove that what happened to him was not really in line with European Union norms," analyst Zsiga said.

Last month, Magyar offered the nomination as president to chess legend Judit Polgar, but she declined after the prime minister faced mounting outrage for not consulting the public as promised.

Magyar has indicated the new president would only serve part of his term, until the completion of a process to replace the Orbán-era Basic Law with a constitution drafted through wide public participation.

Magyar has estimated rewriting the constitution would take one or one and a half years, promising to launch consultations on it next month.

World.title: Istanbul overtakes Heathrow as Europe’s busiest airport after London hub sees passenger numbers fall
World.content:
Heathrow has lost its crown as Europe’s busiest airport, with Istanbul welcoming almost 300,000 more passengers than the London hub in July.

 

The shift comes as Heathrow has seen a summer dip in passenger numbers, particularly on Middle East routes, while its long-running push for a third runway gathers pace.

Figures, released annually by the trade body Airports Council International, reveal that Heathrow was Europe’s busiest airport from 1996 to 2019.

In 2020, it lost its top spot as coronavirus travel restrictions took hold. It regained its title in 2023 and held onto it until this year.

Now, though, the latest figures released by the airport show that 7.86 million passengers passed through its four terminals in July – a relatively low amount.

In contrast, Istanbul airport recorded 8.15 million passengers over the same month, traditionally among the busiest dates for the hubs.

In simple terms, that means Heathrow’s July passenger total saw a 1.5% decrease compared with the same month last year, while Istanbul saw a 2.3% boost when compared to last July.

Heathrow was particularly badly hit by the ongoing Iran-US conflict, with passenger numbers across Middle East routes down 20.2% year-on-year in July.

In a statement, representatives for the airport said the “case for expansion has never been clearer”.

It currently operates its two runways at almost full capacity, and has been seeking government permission to build a third runway for some time now.

Heathrow’s expansion proposal would see it able to process some 150 million passengers per year, up from just under 85 million in 2025.

It’s not clear when – or if – the proposal will be given the go-ahead, though.

Recently sacked Chancellor of the Exchequer Rachel Reeves said she’d hoped for a third runway by 2035, but the UK’s new Prime Minister Andy Burnham seems to be less keen.

He previously said the plans would divert investment “away from the North and traps it in London”.

Despite the dip in passenger numbers, Heathrow is still very busy and popular. 19 July was its busiest day so far this year, with 267,000 passengers recorded.

New airlines have also started serving the airport from July, including Italy’s ITA Airways, Alaska Airlines and Riyadh Air.

World.title: US vaccination executive order: making sense of it
World.content:
President Donald Trump and his Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have long tried to reduce the number of vaccinations available to the US public and even farm animals. The latest move in context.

US President Donald Trump signed another executive order on Monday, August 10, 2026: "Delivering gold standard childhood vaccine recommendations for Americans."

The order reduces the current recommendation of 18 vaccines for children down to 11, which puts it almost in line with the World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations.

As DW reported in May 2025, there are vaccines against 30 infectious diseases. The World Health Organization recommends that every child get vaccinated against 12 of those:

Tuberculosis

Hepatitis B

Polio

Diphtheria

Tetanus

Pertussis (whooping cough)

Haemophilus influenza type B

Pneumococcal disease

Rotavirus

Measles

Rubella

Human papillomavirus

This is the WHO making recommendations for all nations — both rich and poor.

Many poor countries face challenges around access to vaccines at prices they can afford and distributing them safely to people living in remote areas.

Protecting vaccines in Ghana's rising heat To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Rich countries, on the other hand, can afford and therefore usually offer more vaccinations than the WHO's base level of 12. But not all of them do.

Germany, for example, recommends 14 vaccinations for children in their first two years after birth.

Germany no longer recommends the BCG vaccine against tuberculosis (TB), which is on the WHO list. It does recommend vaccination against Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), which is not on the WHO list.

This just goes to show that there are variations around the world. It's not just the US. These variations often depend on which diseases are considered by local health experts to be an ongoing threat to any given community.

Taking the example of TB in Germany: In 1998, the country's Standing Committee on Vaccination (STIKO) decided the risk of TB infections was low, and herd immunity was deemed high enough at 50-80%. Therefore the STIKO stopped recommending the vaccine.

What does Trump's new childhood vaccine recommendation say?

Trump wants to create three distinct categories for vaccination.

The first category includes immunizations recommended for all children: measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type b (meningitis), pneumococcal disease, human papillomavirus and varicella (smallpox).

That removes vaccination against hepatitis B, rotavirus, influenza and RSV from this baseline category that were on the recommended list until now.

These illnesses however can still affect newborns. As we reported in 2022, cases of RSV have risen in the US and Europe. Babies who don't receive the vaccine would remain unprotected against the illness.

By contrast, Germany recommends vaccination for RSV, rotavirus and hepatitis B in a child's first six months.

Trump's executive order also recommends that the combined MMR vaccine for measles, mumps and rubella — which is a global standard — be split into individual jabs, spaced over time.

This appears to be a reflection on long-held rhetoric from the Trump administration suggesting that the combined MMR vaccine causes autism. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) says there is no published evidence to suggest there is any benefit in single jabs.

In fact, its advice on the MMR vaccine states that "the CDC and the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) agree that MMR vaccine is not responsible for recent increases in the number of children with autism."

But Trump and Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have long suggested vaccines are dangerous in general.

Kennedy also thinks that the common painkiller Tylenol causes autism when taken during pregnancy. It is the only painkiller allowed during pregnancy in the US. And as we reported in September 2025, no high-quality scientific evidence substantiated their claim.

Is the US experiencing a vaccine crisis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trump's second category would include immunizations for high-risk groups or populations: respiratory syncytial virus monoclonal antibodies, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, meningococcal B, meningococcal ACWY, and dengue.

The third would include vaccines to be given "based on shared clinical decision-making" — so, doctor and patient or parent of a patient would have to agree. These include: hepatitis A, hepatitis B, rotavirus, meningococcal disease, influenza and COVID-19.

The effect of political — rather than scientific — rhetoric on vaccines

While there's no direct recommendation to ban any vaccine, the second Trump administration has repeatedly attempted to destabilize public consensus over vaccination.

That can cause confusion in the community and rising rates of infection. For example, in July 2026, DW reported how "amnesia" about measles and how dangerous it is had led to a rise in measles infections in the US. People had missed opportunities to get vaccinated because infection rates had been low, but then they rose again.

This is not just the case in North America. Germany has also seen measles infections rise, with experts citing anti-vaccination rhetoric that emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Allowing bird flu to spread

Kennedy however takes his hands-off rhetoric to farming communities, too. In March 2025, DW reported how the health secretary suggested bird flu should be allowed to spread through bird populations, even in places where it had already infected cattle.

Kennedy said it would enable researchers to develop "super" chickens. But instead, more than 150 million birds got infected. Bird flu virus was detected in raw milk. And there were bird-to-human infections as well.

On Monday, when Trump's executive order was released, the AAP's Andrew Racine said it was "not based on 'gold-standard science.' There is no new evidence to justify significant changes to childhood immunization guidance."

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

World.title: Disrupted monsoons force India to face climate threat
World.content:
For generations, India has lived by the rhythm of the southwest monsoon. But with the country hit by dry spells, cloudbursts and deadly floods, climate swings now expose the costs of building for yesterday's weather.

India's southwest monsoon usually arrives around June, brings most of the country's annual rainfall and begins to retreat by September.

Its timing and intensity have always varied, but the broad pattern was predictable enough for farmers, cities and businesses to plan around it. Now, this natural rhythm increasingly seems like a thing of the past.

More than 100 people have been killed across India since late July as heavy monsoon rains triggered floods, landslides and lightning strikes.

The northeastern state of Assam has borne the brunt, with more than 120,000 people affected by flooding. Kerala, Jammu and Kashmir, Bihar and Jharkhand have also reported deaths and widespread disruption.

India's capital New Delhi has also been affected by flooding Image: Sanchit Khanna/Hindustan Times/Sipa USA/picture alliance

The problem is not necessarily that India is receiving more rain. It is the way the rain is arriving: longer dry spells are followed by short bursts of intense rainfall that can overwhelm rivers, drainage systems and hillsides.

El Nino has added to this year's variability but scientists say the longer-term changes are being driven by a changing climate.

Have the monsoons entered a new era?

Akshay Deoras, a senior research scientist with the UK's National Centre for Atmospheric Science and the University of Reading, cautions against describing the Indian monsoon as having entered "a fundamentally different regime."

"Active and break spells have always been part of the monsoon. What appears to be changing is their intensity," Deoras told DW.

He pointed out a warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture, making active spells, or periods of intense rainfall, more intense.

Tidal flooding in Kerala: A crisis no one saw coming To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Madhavan Nair Rajeevan, a climate scientist and former secretary in the Ministry of Earth Sciences, says the change is visible in the behaviour of the monsoon itself.

Average seasonal rainfall, he said, has not shown a systematic long-term change and the monsoon remains a robust natural phenomenon. But the timing, intensity and distribution of rainfall are all noticeably different.

"The characteristics of the Indian monsoon have changed fundamentally," Rajeevan told DW. "We are witnessing an increase in short-duration rainfall extremes, longer dry spells, and changes in the frequency, intensity and distribution of monsoon weather systems."

He believes the rise in extreme rainfall is more than natural variability.

"It represents a structural shift in the monsoon system," he said.

Villages and cities both at risk

India's farmers depend heavily on the timing of rainfall. Long dry spells can disrupt sowing and reduce soil moisture and intense rain can wash away fields and damage crops.

India's cities are also struggling due to rapid construction, as new roads and buildings leave less land to absorb water, thus interfering with natural drainage.

Moreover, after weeks of dry weather, hard, dry soil absorbs less water. When heavy rain finally arrives, more of it floods the rivers and drains instead of replenishing groundwater.

India not stepping up to extreme weather hazard

"The greatest risks increasingly come from short periods of very intense rainfall," Deoras told DW, warning that India's infrastructure is increasingly out of step with this changing threat.

Deoras says drainage systems and flood management are still too often designed around historical seasonal rainfall averages rather than the short, high-impact events that cause the greatest disruption.

He noted that forecasting has improved, but knowing that extreme rain is coming is only useful if authorities act on the warning.

Closing the flood warning gap To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Warnings, he said, need to translate into "timely, impact-based decisions" such as changing school schedules, restricting travel or closing off vulnerable areas before heavy rain arrives.

Ritwick Dutta, an environmental lawyer and managing trustee of the Legal Initiative for Forest and Environment, says the problem goes beyond extreme weather itself.

"It is now scientifically accepted that climate change leads to erratic rainfall patterns. High rainfall over a few days followed by long dry periods during the monsoon," Dutta told DW.

"These trends have been compounded by the fact that the decision-making process in India fails to consider climate change while planning construction projects."

Dutta points to the western city of Pune, where a study by the state government and the Energy and Resources Institute projects a 37% increase in rainfall by 2030. Still, Dutta says this projection has not been adequately incorporated into the city's planning, including its riverfront development.

"Dams, embankments and roads are all likely to suffer major damage due to climate change, and yet we proceed as though climate change is a matter to be discussed only in conferences and workshops," Dutta said.

"We are, in effect, 'weaponizing the environment'," Dutta said.

India-Pakistan floods and the impact of climate change To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Dutta says India's environmental clearance system does not require climate change to be systematically factored into project decisions.

"The concept of 'climate proofing' does not exist here," he said.

Thousands killed in last year's monsoon

The Centre for Science and Environment (CSE) found that extreme weather affected India on 331 of 334 monitored days in 2025, or 99% of the period assessed.

More than 4,000 people died, about 3,000 during the monsoon, while at least 30 states and union territories experienced extreme weather simultaneously for eight consecutive months.

Sunita Narain, director general of the CSE, argues that adaptation therefore needs to become part of the country's development strategy.

"Climate change is no longer a future threat. It is already here in the form of extreme heat, extreme rainfall and increasingly destructive weather events," Narain told DW.

"The challenge is no longer proving the science, but redesigning our economy and infrastructure to survive it," she added.

"Cities, roads, drainage systems and water infrastructure can no longer be designed for yesterday's climate."

Every investment, she says, must be planned for a future of more intense and unpredictable weather.

In her reckoning, India must stop treating each flood as an isolated disaster and start planning for a climate in which such extremes are no longer exceptional.

What can be done against extreme weather?

India is facing a whole new pattern of extreme weather. It can record a rainfall deficit nationally while individual regions are underwater. Farmers can go weeks without useful rain and then lose crops in a few hours. Cities can prepare for an average monsoon and still be overwhelmed by one extraordinary downpour.

"The focus now needs to move beyond documenting and discussing these changes towards developing and implementing effective, sector-specific adaptation strategies," climate scientist and former Indian official Rajeevan said.

That means better flood management in cities, changes in agricultural practices, stronger water-storage systems and infrastructure designed around short-duration extreme rainfall rather than historical averages.

India cannot control the monsoon or El Nino and it cannot stop global warming on its own. It can decide, however, where it builds, how it builds and if its new infrastructure is designed for the climate of its future.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

World.title: Colombia earthquake: Rescuers race to find thousands missing
World.content:
Thousands remain unaccounted for, with many buried under rubble and rescuers yet to reach more isolated communities. The true scale of the destruction is emerging only slowly, with the death toll likely to rise steeply.

Rescuers and volunteers searched through collapsed buildings across western Colombia on Tuesday after a magnitude 7.4 earthquake caused widespread destruction across several major cities a day prior.

The Colombian Association of Capital Cities, known as Asocapitales, put the confirmed death toll at 169 on Tuesday, with 668 people injured.

What do we know about the western Colombia earthquake?

The quake struck near the community of San Jose del Palmar in the western region of Choco on Monday, causing widespread destruction in the cities of Cali, Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo and Buenaventura.

Cali accounted for 85 deaths and Pereira 66, according to the association.

The figures remain incomplete because they largely cover major cities and do not yet include the full toll from rural communities.

More than 3,000 people have been reported missing, with many feared trapped beneath collapsed buildings.

Around 1,600 buildings have been damaged or destroyed. Soldiers, emergency teams and relatives have been clearing debris in dozens of towns and cities, with volunteers forming lines to pass chunks of concrete by hand.

The cities of Pereira, Cali, Quibdo and Manizales remain on red alert because of the scale of the damage.

At least 165 buildings completely collapsed in those cities alone. Hospitals, airports, public utilities and transport systems have also been damaged across several western departments.

The epicenter was near one of Colombia's poorest and most isolated regions. Large parts of the area can be reached only by boat, aircraft or through jungle routes, while damaged roads and other infrastructure are complicating access. That means the full extent of casualties and destruction near the epicenter remains unclear.

How has the world responded?

The United States has offered $15.5 million (€13.42 million) in emergency assistance, while the European Union has activated its Copernicus satellite service to support rescue operations.

The EU has also begun providing emergency assistance following the earthquake, including €100,000 in initial aid through the German Red Cross.

Israel, Mexico, Chile, Argentina and El Salvador have also offered assistance.

The earthquake was felt beyond Colombia, including in parts of Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama.

More than 100 dead in Colombia after major earthquake To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Why was such a deep quake so damaging?

The scale of the destruction was striking because the earthquake struck at a depth of around 100 kilometers (62 miles), where surface shaking would normally be expected to be weaker.

Geologist Raul Perez of Spain's Geological and Mining Institute told EFE news agency that the magnitude 7.4 quake was a particularly complex subduction event involving the Nazca and South American tectonic plates.

He said a "site effect" in some areas amplified the seismic waves as they passed through local geological formations, increasing both the strength and duration of the shaking and worsening damage to buildings.

Perez said the combination of the quake's unusual depth, its magnitude and the local amplification effects made it an event that would need to be studied closely.

Edited by: Rebecca Staudenmaier
